item.title: Holding Hope When Life Has Let You Down
item.description:
Resilience

Holding Hope When Life Has Let You Down

Hope is essential to resilience, but for many people, it no longer feels safe.

Posted July 16, 2026

Key points
  • Repeated setbacks and disappointments can make hope begin to feel risky.
  • Rebuilding hope often involves strengthening self-trust and trust in others.
  • Hope plays a key role in building, practicing, and sustaining resiliency.

Something I’m noticing is that many people are afraid to get their hopes up. When you’ve experienced setbacks and disappointments, and been let down by systems, by people, or even by your own best efforts, hope no longer feels entirely safe to lean into. And yet, we know that it is one of the mightiest contributors to resilience and well-being that we have.

I recently had a conversation with Ross Ellenhorn, psychotherapist, social worker, and author of Ten Reasons Not to Change, that brought language to something I think many people are experiencing: Sometimes people are not lacking hope, they are afraid of it.

His work helps us see that people may exist in very different emotional relationships with hope: some living in despair and disconnected from hope entirely, some grounded in hope and living in a place of being hope-filled, and others fearing hope.

Hope is something quiet but mighty. As Ellenhorn describes it, hope is the capacity to move toward something you yearn for despite uncertainty (Life by Design, 2026). It’s trusting that whatever comes, you’ll find your way through it. Hope changes the lens through which we see the world and allows us to act without guarantees. And when we understand hope this way, we also begin to understand why it can feel risky.

A Fear of Hope

When we hope, we also open ourselves up to disappointment. Maybe it’s a future that didn’t arrive the way we imagined, a relationship that fell apart, or opportunities that disappeared. When people have experienced repeated setbacks, hope starts feeling less like a pathway and more like a risk.

What can look like hopeless behaviour is often not a lack of hope, but a fear of it. His research shows that people who appear stuck can actually carry both high hope and high fear of hope. That internal conflict can lead to anxiety, rumination, and self-blame.

What looks like giving up or resisting change from the outside is often an act of self-protection on the inside. Sometimes thoughts like “I’d rather not try,” “I won’t get excited yet,” or “I’m keeping my expectations low” are signs that hope no longer feels safe. Staying the same becomes a way of guarding hope from being injured again. This can be especially true for those navigating mental health challenges and addictions.

As Ellenhorn shares, in these moments, what people may need most is not pressure to change, but support that helps them build faith in themselves (I can handle disappointment) and faith in others (I won’t be alone in it).

Rebuilding hope often begins with rebuilding trust in ourselves. Trust that even if life does not unfold the way we hoped, we can still adapt, recover, and find our next right step. As we build evidence that we can handle disappointment and uncertainty, hope begins to feel safer. We start to trust not necessarily the outcome, but our ability to navigate whatever comes next. That sense of self-efficacy and personal agency allows us to move toward the future without fearing it quite so much.

article continues after advertisement

What Ellenhorn shares closely connects with the framework I call Everyday Resiliency because resiliency helps us build the inner and relational resources that help us stay connected to hope, even after setbacks, loss, uncertainty, or difficult life experiences.

Hope and Everyday Resiliency

Everyday Resiliency centers on five pillars: belonging, perspective, acceptance, humour, and hope. Each one supports us in unique ways, yet hope is the thread that runs through all of them. It lives inside everything we do to stay well and plays a key role as the most powerful element in building, practicing, and sustaining resiliency.

Hope and Belonging – When we hold hope, we reach toward others. We build connections rooted in trust. We celebrate each other’s wins instead of fearing there won’t be enough to go around. Hope-filled belonging reminds us we are stronger together.

Hope and Perspective – Hope keeps us from being pulled under. It lifts our eyes above immediate difficulty and keeps us focused on the possibility of better. A hopeful perspective doesn’t deny hardship, but it protects our hearts from being driven by fear alone.

Hope and Acceptance – Acceptance isn’t resignation. It’s acknowledging reality while still believing in the possibility of change. Hope within acceptance allows us to face difficult truths without losing sight of our capacity to grow. It’s like a shield and a path at the same time.

Hope and Humour – Hope and humour are complementary forces. Hope keeps us moving forward, and humour lightens the journey. Together, they form one of the most resilient pairings I know. Even in our hardest moments, the ability to find lightness is an act of courage.

A Hopeful Check-In

One practice I share in my book I Hope So is a simple check-in that can help us cultivate hope by working with our controllables while staying committed to our course.

Pause and Reflect: Ask yourself: Where am I feeling the most stress right now? Notice what’s within your control, somewhat within your control, and outside of it. Choose one area within your control or somewhat within your control to carry forward.

Hopeful Reframe: Ask yourself: What is one small thing I can do to feel a little more hopeful about this situation? It might be as simple as sending a message to a friend, taking a 10-minute walk, or making a list of small, manageable tasks.

Anchor in Hope: Say to yourself: “I don’t have to solve everything right now. I just need to take one small step toward hope.” Then visualize how that small step might create a positive ripple.

article continues after advertisement

Final Thoughts

Many of us are moving through our days exhausted, overwhelmed, and uncertain about what the future holds. The world around us may feel turbulent, while our inner world feels tender or fragile. And yet, even when it has been bruised or wrapped in fear, hope remains.

Hope is a force that keeps us moving forward. It encourages us to take small, meaningful steps, even when the outcome isn’t guaranteed. It strengthens our ability to persevere with resiliency and reminds us that we can do hard things.

When we have this trust in ourselves to adapt and overcome, we begin to trust what we cannot yet see and hold onto the possibility of brighter days ahead.

After all, what we do in ordinary time allows us to be extraordinary when called upon. Hope, practiced daily, held gently (and sometimes boldly), and protected with compassion, is how we begin to build and co-create brighter futures.

item.title: 3 Ways Women Settle for Less, and How to Negotiate for More
item.description:
Leadership

3 Ways Women Settle for Less, and How to Negotiate for More

Asking for more at work often means tolerating discomfort and learning from “no.”

Posted July 16, 2026

Key points
  • Women may be judged more harshly than men for initiating salary negotiations.
  • If you ask for less before anyone objects, you're negotiating against yourself.
  • A frown or pause may be a negotiating tactic, not proof you've damaged the relationship.
  • A first “no” often reveals what matters to the other side and makes new possibilities visible.

“I know you’re right. But I can’t ask for that. I don’t want to seem greedy or ungrateful. I know I’d be great at the new job they’re offering me, and they’d have to pay at least as much to hire someone from outside. But I love working here. I don’t want to damage my relationship with them.”

Sound familiar? I’ve heard versions of this from many clients while coaching them through salary negotiations. Even tough-as-nails executives who drive hard bargains with clients and suppliers can turn to jelly when negotiating their own salary.

The “Good Girl” Trap

This tendency isn’t unique to women, but it does appear to be more pronounced among them. Research suggests that gender differences become especially marked when women fear that asking for more will make them seem aggressive or overly demanding.

That fear is not entirely unjustified. But it can create a “good girl” trap: Women reduce their ask before anyone rejects it, interpret ordinary negotiating tension as damage to the relationship, and treat “no” as the end of the conversation rather than its beginning.

1. Reducing the Ask

Instead of asking for what they want, people often ask for what they imagine the other side will accept. Before negotiations begin, they do the other side’s bargaining for them and arrive with a pre-compromised proposal.

This can mean weakening the ask with apologies, offering concessions immediately, filling an uncomfortable silence, or reassuring the other side that you understand if the answer is no.

Instead, decide what you want before discomfort persuades you to want less. Write down your opening request, your realistic goal, and the minimum you will accept. Then make the request—and stop talking!

2. Mistaking Discomfort for Damage

People don’t like being made uncomfortable. Negotiations often involve discomfort, and women who initiate salary negotiations may be penalized more than men.

But a hesitation, frown, or objection is not proof that the relationship itself has been damaged. Expect pauses, pushback, and claims that your request is “difficult.” These may simply be the other person’s opening moves.

As John Kerry once put it, “If it’s a good negotiation, all the parties are uncomfortable.” A negotiation in which neither side experiences discomfort may not have reached the issues that matter most.

3. Hearing “No” as the End, Not the Beginning

Another common mistake is treating “no” as evidence that the negotiation has failed. This tendency is less clearly gendered, although women negotiating for themselves may concede more quickly after encountering resistance.

Former FBI hostage negotiator Chris Voss argues, on the contrary, that a well-handled “no” can reveal the other side's constraints and priorities. Negotiators who pursue that missing information tend to understand the situation better and reach better agreements.

So, treat “no” as data, not a decision. Instead of conceding or arguing, ask: “Which part doesn’t work for you?” “What’s the main obstacle?” “What would have to change for this to become possible?”

You may discover that “no” means not at that price, not on that timetable, or not without someone else’s approval. Curiosity can produce a better counteroffer while showing that you take the other person’s concerns seriously.

The Path to More

Whatever your gender, you don’t have to choose between negotiating firmly and remaining cordial. You just need to stop sacrificing your own needs to avoid pushback. Make the full ask, let the conversation become uncomfortable, and stay curious when the answer is “no.” The path to more begins with the courage to ask and the tenacity to negotiate.

item.title: Why Antidepressants Can Make the Heat More Dangerous
item.description:
SSRIs

Why Antidepressants Can Make the Heat More Dangerous

Some antidepressants can increase the risk of overheating and dehydration.

Posted July 16, 2026

Key points
  • Antidepressants can interfere with the body's ability to regulate temperature.
  • Heat-related symptoms range from mild discomfort to life-threatening heat stroke.
  • Simple precautions can significantly lower the risk during hot weather.
Source: Orna / Pixabay

It is summer in the Northern Hemisphere, and in a few months it will be in the South as well. But for those taking antidepressants, the hottest months of the year do not always bring only sunshine and outdoor activities.

Heat intolerance is a common complaint among antidepressant users, and symptoms often become more noticeable during periods of high temperatures.

SSRIs (selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors) and SNRIs (serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors) are the antidepressants most commonly associated with heat intolerance, although people taking medications from other classes, such as tricyclic antidepressants, may also experience symptoms during hot weather.

Mechanism of the effect

Some antidepressants affect the body's ability to regulate temperature, increasing the risk of heat-related symptoms such as dizziness, nausea, headaches, fatigue, and dehydration.

The way this happens depends on the type of antidepressant. SSRIs including Prozac (fluoxetine), Celexa (citalopram), Lexapro (escitalopram), and Zoloft (sertraline), and SNRIs including Cymbalta (duloxetine) and Effexor (venlafaxine), can cause excessive sweating, a side effect known as secondary hyperhidrosis.

In the case of tricyclic antidepressants, the ability to regulate body temperature through sweating can be affected in two ways: in some cases, there is an increase in sweating, while in others, there is a reduction. When sweating is reduced, this occurs because of the anticholinergic effect of these medications.

The mechanism behind secondary hyperhidrosis still needs to be better understood, but the most accepted hypothesis is that serotonin, whose concentration increases with the use of these antidepressants, acts on the hypothalamus, the body's temperature control center. As a result, the hypothalamus may activate one of the body's cooling mechanisms: sweating.

This explains the profuse sweating that some people experience during hot weather. But it also increases the risk of overheating because, when a person becomes dehydrated after losing large amounts of fluid through sweat, the body's ability to cool itself becomes less effective.

Symptoms that deserve attention

Heat waves, or even the high temperatures typical of summer, can pose health risks, especially for people taking antidepressants.

The most common problem is dehydration, which can occur when fluid losses from heat and sweating are not adequately replaced. The main symptoms include dry mouth, dark and strong-smelling urine, headache, dizziness, tiredness, and intense thirst.

If left untreated, dehydration can progress to heat stroke. In this condition, the body can no longer regulate its temperature effectively. The signs are quite different from those of simple dehydration, and include hot and dry skin (often with no sweating at all), mental confusion, slurred speech, a rapid heartbeat, and a very high body temperature.

Heat stroke is a medical emergency and requires immediate medical attention.

How to stay safe

The first thing to remember is not to stop taking your medication on your own. Abruptly stopping antidepressants can cause unpleasant and sometimes severe withdrawal symptoms.

A few simple strategies can help reduce the discomfort and health risks associated with taking antidepressants in hot weather:

  • Avoid sun exposure during the hottest hours of the day whenever possible.
  • Drink water regularly. It may also help to eat water-rich fruits, such as watermelon, since some people report that antidepressants reduce their sensation of thirst.
  • Avoid alcohol and caffeine, as both can contribute to fluid loss.
  • Wear lightweight, breathable clothing to help your body stay cool.

These recommendations apply to everyone during hot weather, but they are especially important for people taking antidepressants.

Another point to keep in mind is the risk of electrolyte imbalance, since sweating causes the body to lose salts such as sodium and potassium. In addition to staying hydrated, it is important to maintain a light, balanced diet. If you notice signs of electrolyte loss, such as muscle cramps, weakness, or confusion, drinks containing electrolytes may also help, as long as they are consumed in moderation.

If you take antidepressants and have not yet discussed this issue with your doctor, it is worth bringing it up at your next appointment. The most important thing is to recognize your body's warning signs and act early, before mild symptoms develop into a more serious condition.

item.title: GLP-1 Journeys: Beyond Weight Loss, Becoming Someone New
item.description:
Health

GLP-1 Journeys: Beyond Weight Loss, Becoming Someone New

Why the deepest changes on a GLP-1 journey often aren't visible on a scale.

Posted July 16, 2026

Key points
  • GLP-1 medicines are used mostly for weight loss. But the changes they produce are often deeply personal.
  • The personal and psychological changes people experience using GLP-1s are frequently unexpected.
  • GLP-1 users should anticipate personal changes and take ownership to guide them during treatment.

Jordan began her GLP-1 journey the way she approaches most things: methodically. She found Zepbound1 through social media, researched it with the same attention she brings to her client projects, and started tracking everything from week 1: weight, waist-hip measurements, weekly photos, energy levels, mood ratings. She had spreadsheets. Benchmarks. Jordan treated her GLP-1 journey like a numbers game, until it started making moves she didn't anticipate.

Before Zepbound, she estimates she spent two to three hours a day thinking about food (e.g., what to order, whether she'd been disciplined enough to justify what she was craving). Jordan assumed this was just what it felt like to be a person in her 20s who loved food and had complicated feelings about her body. Then, a few weeks in, "the food thoughts just stopped," she says. "Not completely, but mostly. And that was the beginning of a whole series of changes I didn't expect."

Jordan had started her treatment to lose weight. She didn't realize she was about to enter a whole different life.

The GLP-1 Assumption Most People Bring

Most people starting a GLP-1 medicine carry some version of the same assumption: I'm going to change on the outside, and stay who I am on the inside. My body will change. Who I am underneath, however, will remain the same as it is now.

It's a reasonable assumption, and it's also not how profound life experiences tend to work. Nobody expects to graduate college as exactly the person who arrived as a freshman. Nobody finishes military boot camp, a dedicated year with a personal trainer, or a training block for a marathon, and reports back that nothing changed except their fitness metrics. We already understand, from many other types of significant life experiences, that the process affects the person far beyond the narrow starting goal. GLP-1 medicines belong in that same transformative experience category. Yet few currently realize this when initiating treatment.

What Actually Changes With GLP-1 Medicines

Food noise is perhaps the most common example of a dramatic and often unexpected change. GLP-1 medicines reduce the mental preoccupation with food that many people don't even recognize as excessive until it's suddenly diminished.2 But the reach of GLP-1 medicines turns out to extend well past food. Whether it is reducing cravings for alcohol and nicotine, interest in gambling and compulsive behaviors, or even influencing sexual desire, research increasingly suggests that GLP-1 medicines influence the biological machinery of wanting itself.3-4 Change a person's wants, and you do not merely alter their behavior. More deeply, you are also rewiring their interests, likes, preferences, and even values.

GLP-1 changes also extend into some of the most personal domains: mood and thought.5 GLP-1 receptors are distributed throughout brain regions involved in emotional regulation and memory. Jordan felt this firsthand at her company's holiday party, an event she used to spend in reserved self-surveillance—monitoring what she ate, how she looked eating it, and whether she was taking up the right amount of space. This year, she says, "I talked to people. Real conversations." Partway through the evening, she realized she hadn't thought about food or her body once.

The GLP-1 treatment experience also affected how Jordan wanted to be seen by others. She'd built a following over three years of curated social media posts—food shots, design work, candid moments with friends. Four months into treatment, she'd posted just twice. "I don't know how to present myself right now," she said at the time. "The person in my old photos doesn't look like me anymore. But the person I am now doesn't feel entirely like me either." Like many others using GLP-1 medicines, Jordan's sense of self was changing. Over time, these inner changes rippled ever further into her outer lifestyle and relationships.

Be the Captain of Your Changes, Not the Passenger

Here's the empowering reframe: If GLP-1 medicines are changing us on the inside as well as the outside, the most important question is who is directing the changes. Are you the captain guiding the changes toward a chosen destination, or a passenger leaving the result to chance?

Think about the people who navigate other major transformations well, the ones who finish a demanding training program, or a stretch of real therapeutic work, and come out the other side somewhere they actually meant to go. They rarely leave it entirely to chance. A good coach, a good therapist, a good mentor typically begins by asking some version of the same questions: What's your outcome? Who are you hoping to be when this is finished? Not as a rigid script to follow, but as a value-based compass to steer the journey.

Unfortunately, GLP-1 treatment rarely arrives from the prescriber with these questions attached. The physician conversation covers dosing schedules and side effects, and frequently little else. It doesn't usually ask what kind of person you're hoping to become or what kind of life you wish to lead. That is a critical gap to fill, and filling it with your own personal intention is superior to leaving it to accident.

A Practical Way to Start

The starting point for charting personal changes during GLP-1 treatment doesn't need to be complicated. Giving some honest thought to what you really want across a few different life domains can be a simple and practical way to guide your GLP-1 journey. The "Vision Map" exercise below is a brief tool to ask (and track) precisely these types of personal change questions.

GLP-1 journey vision map
Source: Thomas Rutledge/PowerPoint

Jordan, Five Months In

Jordan deleted four of her five tracking apps in May. The one she kept isn't for weight. It tracks her sleep, the single metric she found most reliably connected to how she actually felt each day.

She still photographs her Saturday cooking, though her images are different: less rehearsed, more likely to show the transparent mess of a kitchen mid-process than just the performative finished dish. She's not sure when that changed. She suspects it has something to do with caring more about the experience and less about its documentation.

"I came into this thinking it was about how I looked," she says. "Now I realize it's more about how I live."
